title: Memory Management & Garbage Collection
summary: Every program borrows memory and must give it back. Who tracks that — you or the runtime — shapes your bugs, your latency tails, and your interview answers.

blocks.markdown:
Memory management is deciding when a chunk of heap memory is no longer needed and can be reused.

- **Stack** frees itself on function return — automatic, fast, no work for you.
- **Heap** is the hard problem: someone must decide when its memory is dead.
- That someone is **you** (manual `malloc`/`free`) or an **algorithm** (reference counting or tracing GC).
- Everything below is variations on *how do we know an object is dead, and how cheaply*.

blocks.subTitle: Which scheme to reach for
blocks.markdown:
Pick the model that matches your latency and control needs.

| If you need… | Reach for… |
|---|---|
| Max control, hard real-time | Manual / arenas |
| Prompt, deterministic cleanup | Reference counting (ARC) |
| No cycle leaks, less mental load | Tracing GC (JVM, Go) |
| Low pauses at scale | Concurrent GC (ZGC, Go) |
| Highest raw throughput | Parallel STW GC |

blocks.subTitle: Stack vs heap
blocks.markdown:
A function call pushes a **stack frame**; returning pops it with one pointer move.

- **Stack** — locals, args, return address; fixed size, freed automatically. ~1 ns to push.
- **Heap** — anything dynamic-sized or outliving its function. ~20–100 ns to allocate, and *freeing is the open question*.
- A local `int` lives on the stack; a `new`/`malloc` object lives on the heap, with the stack holding only a **pointer** to it.
- Stack overflow = too-deep recursion; heap exhaustion = out-of-memory.

blocks.subTitle: Manual: malloc, free, four bugs
blocks.markdown:
In C, `malloc` reserves heap bytes and `free` returns them — until the bookkeeping goes wrong.

- **Leak** — allocate, never free; process grows until OOM.
- **Use-after-free** — free, then keep using the pointer; corruption and the #1 exploit source.
- **Double free** — free the same pointer twice; corrupts the allocator's free-list.
- **Dangling pointer** — any pointer outliving its target, including one to a popped stack local.

These bugs are **non-local** — allocation and misuse can be thousands of lines apart, which is why automation won.

blocks.subTitle: Reference counting & cycles
blocks.markdown:
Each object counts incoming references: `count++` on assign, `count--` on drop, free at zero.

- **Upside** — cleanup is prompt and deterministic, freed the instant the last reference drops, no pauses.
- **Fatal flaw** — **cycles**. If A points to B and B points to A, both stay at 1 forever even when unreachable. A leak.
- **Python** uses ref counting plus a cycle-detecting tracer to mop these up.
- **Swift ARC** doesn't, so you break cycles manually with `weak` references.

blocks.subTitle: Tracing GC: reachability
blocks.markdown:
A tracing collector ignores counts and computes **reachability** from the **roots** — stack variables, CPU registers, globals.

- Follow every pointer from the roots; what you reach is **live**, the rest is **garbage** — cycles included.
- **Mark-and-sweep** — mark reachable, sweep the rest. Simple, but leaves the heap **fragmented**.
- **Mark-compact** — mark, then slide live objects together. Fixes fragmentation; costs pointer fix-ups.
- **Copying** — split heap in two, copy survivors to the other half, free the old half wholesale. Cost scales with *live* data.

blocks.subTitle: Generational GC
blocks.markdown:
The **weak generational hypothesis**: most objects die young. Generational GC exploits it.

- Split the heap into a **young gen** (new objects) and an **old gen** (survivors).
- Collect the young gen **often and cheaply** with a copying collector — most of it is already dead.
- Survivors of a few minor GCs are **promoted** to the old gen, collected **rarely**.
- A **write barrier** records old→young pointers in a remembered set, so they count as extra roots for the young collection.

blocks.subTitle: Generational GC walkthrough
blocks.markdown:
Trace a request handler that builds a cycle, then returns.

```python
def handle_request():
    a = Node()      # young
    b = Node()      # young
    a.next = b      # a -> b
    b.prev = a      # b -> a  (a cycle!)
    return          # a, b now unreachable
```

- After Eden fills, a **minor GC** scans roots — `a` and `b` are no longer on any stack.
- The tracer never visits the dead `a`/`b` island, so the **cycle is reclaimed**; ref counting would leak it.
- Minor GC copies only the few survivors, so its cost scales with survivors, not allocations.

blocks.subTitle: Stop-the-world vs concurrent
blocks.markdown:
The mark phase needs a consistent heap snapshot, so the simplest fix is **stop-the-world**: pause all threads, collect, resume.

- A full STW GC on a multi-GB heap can freeze an app for **hundreds of ms to seconds** — death for latency.
- **Incremental** — break collection into small chunks: many short pauses instead of one long one.
- **Concurrent** — run GC threads alongside the app using **tri-color marking** (white/gray/black) plus a write barrier.
- ZGC, Shenandoah, and Go keep pauses **under 1 ms** even on huge heaps.

blocks.subTitle: The dimensions you trade on
blocks.markdown:
You can't max everything — GC design is picking a point on these axes.

| Dimension | The tension |
|---|---|
| Throughput vs pause | Lower pauses cost more GC CPU |
| Determinism vs ease | Manual frees at a known time; tracing eventually |
| Headroom | A GC wants ~2–5× the live set to run well |
| Fragmentation vs moving | Non-moving fragments; moving fixes pointers |

Manual gives control and zero pauses but the four bugs; GC removes the bugs but takes away timing control.

blocks.subTitle: Plain-English rules
blocks.markdown:
Match the collector to the workload.

- **Tiny pauses on a large heap** → concurrent collector (ZGC, Shenandoah, Go).
- **Throughput batch job**, a 1 s pause is fine → parallel STW collector; it finishes total work fastest.
- **Hard real-time or tiny hardware** → manual or arena allocation; GC timing is disqualifying.
- **Cycles rare, prompt cleanup matters** (closing handles) → reference counting (RAII/ARC).
- **Millions of short-lived objects** → generational GC with a large enough young gen.

blocks.subTitle: Real systems & monitoring
blocks.markdown:
How the big runtimes choose, and what to watch in prod.

- **JVM** — generational; **G1** hits a pause-time target you set, **ZGC/Shenandoah** give sub-ms pauses on huge heaps.
- **Go** — concurrent, *non-generational* mark-sweep; escape analysis keeps short-lived objects on the stack. `GOGC` trades memory for CPU.
- **CPython** — ref counting plus a generational cycle collector. **Rust** — compile-time ownership, memory safety with zero GC cost.
- **Monitor**: pause time (p99/max), GC frequency, allocation rate, and old-gen occupancy after each major GC ([b05-caching](b05-caching.md)).

The misconceptions that bite in interviews and production.

- **"GC means I never think about memory."** A growing cache or unremoved listener stays *reachable* — a logical leak GC won't touch.
- **"Nulling a reference frees it now."** In tracing GC it only becomes *eligible*; reclaimed at the next GC, never synchronously.
- **"Ref counting and tracing are the same."** Ref counting is prompt but blind to cycles; tracing handles cycles but reclaims late.
- **"A bigger heap is always better."** Rarer GCs, but each scans more and can pause longer, and it hides leaks.
- **"Pauses scale with heap size."** Mark cost scales with the *live set*; a 90%-garbage heap collects fast.
